title: “My husband hired 40 guards to keep me out of the hospital while his mistress gave birth.”

blocks.text: Grant Whitcomb believed money could control everything.
At thirty-six, he was the billionaire founder and CEO of Whitcomb Global, a technology and investment empire worth more than $8 billion.
And for nine years, he had been married to Willa Whitcomb.
And, in Grant’s opinion, completely dependent on him.
That last assumption would become the most expensive mistake of his life.
For almost two years, Grant had been having an affair with Sloane Mercer, his thirty-year-old chief of staff.
Everyone around Grant suspected something was wrong.
Everyone except Willa—or at least, that’s what Grant believed.
Grant’s secret suddenly became impossible to hide.
But instead of ending his marriage, he decided to humiliate his wife.
On the morning Sloane went into labor, Grant personally called the security director at the private hospital.
“Sir, your wife is legally listed as your emergency contact.”
“Forty guards,” Grant snapped. “I want forty guards stationed around that floor. Nobody lets Willa through.”
“And if she comes crying, begging to see me?”
“She needs to understand that she’s no longer important.”
She didn’t even ask whether the baby had been born.
For nine years, Willa had been predictable.
She stood beside him during company announcements.
She defended him whenever tabloids questioned his business practices.
And whenever Grant threatened to leave, Willa always seemed terrified.
At 3:17 p.m., Sloane gave birth to a healthy baby boy.
Grant stood beside her bed, holding the newborn.
The next morning, he planned to announce the birth publicly.
But before he could, his phone exploded with notifications.
“Someone just sold $1.5 billion worth of shares.”
“There was a transfer of shares six months ago.”
“My wife doesn’t control that much stock.”
“Before your marriage, Willa’s father placed a substantial block of Whitcomb Global shares into a private family trust.”
“Approximately eighteen percent of the company.”
That was enough to make Willa one of the company’s largest individual shareholders.
The attorney explained that Willa had quietly transferred the voting rights to an independent investment group months earlier.
“Because the trust was legally independent.”
Six months earlier, Willa had asked him a strange question.
She had been sitting across from him at breakfast.
“If I ever stopped being your wife,” she’d asked, “would you still respect me?”
At the time, he thought she was being sentimental.
And she had already known what she was going to do.
But the most disturbing thing was what she had left behind.
It sat neatly on the dining table beside a handwritten note.
His hands trembled as he unfolded the paper.
For the first time in nine years, he felt afraid.
Then his assistant rushed into the room.
“The board called an emergency meeting.”
A group of institutional investors had submitted a proposal demanding changes to Whitcomb Global’s leadership.
And they had enough votes to force a shareholder vote.
The investment group controlling the shares Willa had transferred was leading the campaign.
The group’s managing director was a man named Elias Vale.
Elias had once been one of his biggest competitors.
Five years earlier, Grant had forced Elias out of a major acquisition.
He had assumed the man disappeared from the industry.
“You have something that belongs to my wife.”
“Ask why your wife knew you were going to betray her before you did.”
Then Elias said something that made his blood run cold.
“Pull every trust document. Everything. Now.”
Minutes later, an encrypted file arrived.
The trust wasn’t created six months ago.
It had existed since before his marriage.
And the original beneficiary agreement contained a clause Grant had never seen.
